Sound the Alarm : IFF’s First Read on MeitY's Draft IT Rules Second Amendment, 2026

New Delhi, 30 March 2026

On 30 March 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology published proposed amendments to the IT Rules, 2021, inviting public comments by 14 April,  a comment period of barely fifteen days for changes with far reaching consequences for free speech and intermediary governance in India. We have conducted a quick review of the draft amendments. Despite being presented as "clarificatory and procedural," they represent a dangerous expansion of executive power over online speech.

We wish to state at the outset that these proposed amendments need to be immediately withdrawn and every member in our citizenry should demand their roll back and stand with the Constitution of India. These proposed amendments come at a time of fear and increased government directed censorship, especially of online political speech that includes parody and satire of the government, including the Prime Minister.

In brief the five changes are listed below:

1. Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h): Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law.

2. Rule 3(4): Insertion of a new clause that mandates intermediary compliance with MeitY-issued clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines, making such compliance a condition for retaining safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act. These are not anchored to the rule making powers of the IT Act, 2000 and provide uncanalised power to MEITY despite it stating otherwise.

3. Rule 8(1) proviso: A substitution in the proviso that expands applicability of MIB’s oversight mechanism in Part III of the rules to:  (1) intermediaries and (2) users who are not “publishers” and post/share news and current affairs content online. This oversight mechanism contains the blocking powers of MIB by way of Rule 14 (Inter-Departmental Committee), Rule 15 (Procedure for issuing directions to block), and Rule 16 (Emergency blocking provisions).

4. Rule 14(2) : A substitution that expands the scope of the IDC from hearing "complaints or grievances" to hearing "matters", including those referred by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

5. Rule 14(5) : Replaces "complaints or grievances" with "the matter" in relation to IDC examination and recommendations.

A massive expansion of an unconstitutional censorship and regulatory power

First and most concerningly, Rule 3(4) creates a sweeping power for MeitY to issue binding instruments which are not anchored in law such as clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines that intermediaries must comply with as a condition of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act.

The Supreme Court's 2015 judgment in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, remains the foundational precedent governing intermediary liability. It constrains the proposed amendments in several ways. First, the court read down Section 79(3)(b) to require that "actual knowledge" of unlawful content must come through a court order or government notification. Any Rule 3(4) making MeitY, "clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs", lower the constitutional threshold for intermediary due diligence obligations.

Further, the settled principle in Indian administrative law, reaffirmed in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) 1 SCC 641 and Confederation of Ex-Servicemen Associations v. Union of India (2006) 8 SCC 399, is that delegated legislation must remain within the four corners of the parent statute.  It is important to note that the rule-making power under Section 87(1) of the IT Act is confined to, "carry[ing] out the provisions" of the Act. Section 87(2)(zg) authorizes rules for intermediary guidelines under Section 79(2), and Section 87(2)(z) for blocking procedures under Section 69A(2). Justice Chandurkar's judgement in the Kunal Kamra case clearly found the FCU amendment was not properly referable to either provision. Hence, any Rule 3(4) mandating compliance with MeitY advisories would face identical challenges since they create substantive new obligations not contemplated by Sections 79 or 87.

Even though Rule 3(4)(b)(ii) states that such, “advisories” etc. need to, “clearly specify the statutory provision or legal basis under which it is issued”, since these are not required to be published or made public there is every likelihood these will be issued with secrecy and hence may just in a tautological manner refer back to Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. This is similar to a logical fallacy in which it is clearly observable that a student is cheating on an exam who then claims that they may be permitted to continue cheating since they are stating at the same time they are not cheating. 

The practical effect of Rule 3(4) is that intermediaries face a perpetual compliance threat. Any failure to comply with any MeitY-issued instrument, however vague, however rapidly issued may cost them their safe harbour. The response for an intermediary is over-compliance and over-censorship.

Circumventing existing stay orders

The original proviso to Rule 8(1) stated that Part III applied to intermediaries only "for the purposes of rules 15 and 16"  i.e., content blocking directions and emergency blocking. The amended proviso now extends this to Rule 14, bringing intermediaries and user-generated news/current affairs content under the jurisdiction of the Inter-Departmental Committee.

Under Rules 9(1) and 9(3) of the 2021 IT Rules, there is a Code of Ethics compliance requirement and the three-tier grievance redressal mechanism, both of which were stayed by the Bombay High Court on 14 August 2021 as prima facie violative of Article 19(1)(a) and ultra vires the IT Act. On the oversight mechanism in Rules 14, 15, and 16, the Bombay High Court granted the petitioners to seek relief on this rule when an Inter Departmental Committee is established. The Madras High Court affirmed this stay as having pan-India effect in its order of 16 September 2021 in T.M. Krishna v. Union of India, observing that "an oversight mechanism to control the media by the government may rob the media of its independence." 

Both these cases, along with other cases challenging various provisions of the 2021 IT Rules, are now pending adjudication before the Delhi High Court.

The expansion of Rule 8(1) to cover Rules 14, 15, and 16 is an attempt to expand the blocking powers of MIB to both intermediaries and users who are not “publishers” but post news and current affairs content online. The IDC can now examine "matters" relating to user-generated news content on intermediary platforms without the Code of Ethics framework having been adjudicated as constitutional; the government effectively obtains the content oversight machinery that three High Courts found illegal, through a different procedural door.

Transforming the IDC from Grievance Body to Censorship Apparatus

The original Rule 14(2) required the IDC to hear "complaints regarding violation or contravention of the Code of Ethics." The amended version removes this requirement entirely. 

The IDC now hears:
(a) grievances arising from decisions at Level I or II; or
(b) "matters" referred to by the Ministry.

Clause (b) is unconstrained since, (a) there is no requirement that the "matter" arise from a complaint, (b) no requirement that the "matter" relate to a Code of Ethics violation; and (c) no requirement that the affected party be heard before the referral. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting can, on its own motion, refer any content-related "matter" to the IDC. 

The cumulative effect of the amendments to Rules 8 and 14 is to reconstruct the oversight machinery that the Bombay and Madras High Courts found constitutionally suspect, in a form designed to evade the existing interim orders. The IDC, previously limited to the three-tier complaints process under the stayed Rules 9(3), 12, and 13 framework, now operates as a free-standing censorship committee that can take up "matters" referred by the executive.

Increased user surveillance through mandatory data retention directions

Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law. For instance, the mandatory data retention of user data beyond 180 days within Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h) may be prescribed for longer periods and other purposes raising risks of surveillance and even potentially data leaks of sensitive data that is stored for longer periods of time. Government mandates for data retention as to their legal authority and hence period of retention will be beyond those contained under the IT Act.

SOS for Digital Rights 

IFF urges an urgent rollback!

We are alarmed by the continuing expansion of unchecked executive power that is opposed to the Constitution of India. The present actions of MEITY smack of digital authoritarianism and we call on them to withdraw these proposed amendments. 

The proper course is to await judicial determination of the pending challenges, respect interim protections granted by constitutional courts, and pursue regulatory objectives through parliamentary legislation rather than subordinate instruments that exceed the parent statute.

If not withdrawn, IFF will file a detailed response before the comment deadline. We call upon all stakeholders to submit their objections before 14 April 2026 at itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in

Statement : The blocking of BitChat's code on GitHub is unconstitutional and authoritarian. 

New Delhi, 24 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the order issued by the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs, directing GitHub to remove the code repositories of BitChat. 

The order, Notice No. 11072601011432, was issued at 11:16 pm on 23 July 2026 under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021. The order directs GitHub to disable access to three repositories, including the Android application and its release files, within three hours. It threatens the platform with loss of safe harbour and criminal prosecution. No copy was published by the Government of India. The public learnt of it from a post by @jack, whose team develops BitChat. Censorship in India now comes to light through disclosure by the censored.

Since 17 July 2026, the Ministry of Home Affairs has suspended mobile internet around Jantar Mantar as per public reports about five times, most recently within a 1.5 kilometre radius from 4 pm until midnight on 23 July. That radius takes in Janpath and parts of Connaught Place. Reports describe signal jammers at the protest site and people walking two kilometres before their phones work. Inside that zone a student separated from her group during a detention drive cannot send a message to say where she is. Thousands of students and young people have camped at Jantar Mantar since June, seeking accountability for examination irregularities. Permission for their march to Parliament was refused. Metro stations were shut and also internet connectivity has been blocked.

BitChat is an open source application built for exactly this situation. It passes messages from phone to phone over Bluetooth, without mobile networks or a central server. It is striking that the order does not identify a single unlawful message. It objects to what BitChat is. In its own words, the application is dangerous because it enables communication "even during network restrictions" and can "circumvent lawful restrictions" during "internet shutdowns". Hence, the government's objection is that citizens can speak to one another while it has switched the internet off. 

The order is illegal on at least four grounds. 

1. Section 79(3)(b) is not a blocking power. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down the provision. Intermediaries may be required to act only on a court order, or a government notification confined to the grounds under Article 19(2) of the Constitution. Blocking is governed exclusively by Section 69A and the Blocking Rules, 2009, which require a hearing and reasons recorded in writing, subject to review. Directions issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal evade these safeguards, and constitutional challenges to this parallel regime are pending before High Courts. 

2. The reasons in the order are circular. The order asserts that the repositories contain "information which is prohibited under any law" without naming any such information, and rests on what the application is "capable of" enabling. Anticipated misuse of a communications tool is not a lawful basis to prohibit the tool. By this logic a telephone exchange could be sealed. 

3. The order cites Section 43 of the IT Act, a civil compensation provision, alongside conspiracy and abetment offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, against a platform that hosts code. 

4. A three hour deadline issued close to midnight forecloses legal assessment and recourse, and fails the proportionality standard in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637.

The order also fails on its own terms as deleting a repository does not delete the application from any phone that carries it, and the mesh keeps functioning without servers. What the takedown actually prevents is scrutiny of the underlying code.

IFF demands that the Government of India:

1. Withdraw Notice No. 11072601011432 dated 23 July 2026 issued to GitHub.
2. Publish every takedown direction issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal, with the reasons recorded for each.
3. Restore full connectivity around Jantar Mantar, publish all suspension orders, and disclose the legal authority for the deployment of jammers.

We stand with the developers and the young protesters whose speech this order seeks to silence.

The Kerala High Court on Tuesday (28 April) issued notice on a plea filed by Madhyamam Broadcasting Limited, broadcaster of Media One news channel, challenging blocking of its official Facebook page in India.

Justice K.V. Jayakumar issued the notice to the respondents and directed the Central government and Meta to file counter affidavits.

The petitioner, contends that its Facebook page was abruptly rendered “not available in India” on April 23, 2026, following a notification citing a request from the Government of India or law enforcement under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000.

According to the petition, the blocking has effectively cut off access to MediaOne's digital content for Indian users, disrupting its online operations and causing significant financial loss.

The broadcaster states that its Facebook page, active since 2011, is a key platform for disseminating news and public interest content and generates substantial revenue estimated at around ₹25 lakh per month.

The petitioner alleges that the action was taken without disclosure of any blocking order under Section 69A of the IT Act, communication of reasons or prior notice or opportunity of hearing.

The petitioner argues that the actions of the respondents is a complete disregard of the mandatory statutory safeguards and constitutional limitations governing online content regulation.

The Petitioner further submitted that the Section 79(3)(b) invoked in the notification, does not confer independent powers to block content. Instead, it only outlines circumstances in which intermediaries lose safe harbour protection.

The petitioner relies on the Supreme Court's ruling in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India [(2015) 5 SCC 1], which held that “actual knowledge” for content takedown must arise only through a court order or a valid government blocking order under Section 69A.

The petition contends that no such court order or Section 69A direction has been disclosed and argues that intermediaries cannot act on informal or undisclosed executive communications.

The petitioner has also challenged the scope of the restriction, arguing that the law permits blocking only of “specific and identifiable content,” not entire accounts or pages.

The blanket disabling of its Facebook page, it claims, is excessive, disproportionate, and contrary to the statutory framework under the IT Act and the Blocking Rules, 2009.

Further, the petition points to the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, which require that blocking directions be content-specific and not result in cessation of operations.

It is further submitted that the blocking violates the petitioner's fundamental rights under Articles 14, 19(1)(a), and 19(1)(g), as well as its property rights under Article 300A of the Constitution of India.

The petitioner has thus sought to set aside the blocking of its Facebook page, declare the action illegal and unconstitutional, direct restoration of access within India, and ensure compliance with statutory safeguards for any future content regulation.

The Court has issued the notice to the respondents and has posted the matter to 5 MAy for further consideration.

Prominent Malayalam news channel MediaOne TV has approached the Kerala High Court challenging the blocking of its Facebook page, alleging that the action was arbitrary and in violation of Supreme Court rulings as well as the Information Technology Act.

The petition states that the Facebook page “MediaOne TV” was restricted on Friday, with access blocked specifically for users in India. The channel argued that the page was blocked without citing any specific content or violation.

While Facebook has the authority to remove content that violates its policies or pursuant to legal orders, the petition contends that it does not have the power to block an entire page.

According to MediaOne, the only explanation provided by Facebook was that the action was taken “based on a request from law enforcement agencies or the Union of India.”

Following this, the channel moved the High Court seeking relief against the action.

Despite the restriction in India, the page remains accessible outside the country, and administrative functions such as uploading news and videos have not been affected.

Earlier, in January 2022, the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting barred MediaOne TV from broadcasting, citing “national security reasons” and denial of security clearance by the Ministry of Home Affairs.

However, in April 2023, the Supreme Court of India quashed the ban, observing that national security claims cannot be made “out of thin air” without material evidence, and that criticism of government policies does not render a channel “anti-national.”

🚨 BIG: Government of India has unveiled one of the most comprehensive legal frameworks to combat AI-generated deepfakes, synthetic media, misinformation and unlawful online content.

The framework brings together the IT Act, 2000, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, IT Rules, 2021, the 2026 IT Rules amendments, and the IndiaAI Governance Guidelines to strengthen digital safety and platform accountability.

Key highlights:

🔹 Mandatory AI Labelling: Platforms must clearly label AI-generated or synthetic content with traceable metadata so users can identify manipulated content and prevent deception.

🔹 Fastest Takedown Timelines Yet: Removal of unlawful content after a valid government or court notice has been reduced from 36 hours to just 3 hours. Grievance redressal timelines have also been tightened—from 72 hours to 36 hours, and 24 hours to 2 hours for sensitive content such as nudity, impersonation and similar categories.

🔹 IT Act, 2000: Covers penalties for computer-related offences, identity theft (Sec. 66C), online impersonation (66D), privacy violations (66E), publishing obscene or sexually explicit content (Secs. 67 & 67A), empowers blocking of unlawful content under Sec. 69A, removal directions under Sec. 79, and enables police investigation under Secs. 78 & 80.

🔹 Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: Covers cheating by personation (Sec. 319), forgery through false electronic records (Sec. 336), spreading false reports or misinformation causing public mischief (Sec. 353), and organised cybercrime involving deepfake content (Sec. 111).

🔹 Strict Platform Obligations: Intermediaries must not host or share content that infringes rights, invades privacy, promotes hate or violence, harms children, violates intellectual property, misleads users about message origin, knowingly spreads false information, impersonates individuals (including using AI), threatens India's sovereignty, security or public order, or violates any applicable law.

🔹 Greater Accountability for Social Media Platforms: Significant Social Media Intermediaries (SSMIs) must assist law enforcement in tracing originators of serious content, deploy automated tools to detect unlawful content, publish compliance reports, appoint grievance and compliance officers, maintain India-based compliance infrastructure, and provide user verification, appeals and fair hearing mechanisms.

🔹 Zero Tolerance for Harmful AI: Platforms are now explicitly required to prevent AI-generated child sexual abuse material, non-consensual intimate imagery, deepfakes, AI impersonation, harmful synthetic media and other unlawful AI-generated content using reasonable technical measures and automated detection systems.

🔹 Legal Consequences: Failure to comply with the IT Rules can result in intermediaries losing their Section 79 safe-harbour protection, exposing them to prosecution and legal action under applicable laws.

🔹 Robust Enforcement Ecosystem: The framework will be enforced through Grievance Appellate Committees (GACs), the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), the SAHYOG Portal, the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, and law enforcement agencies. Citizens can report cybercrime and deepfakes through the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, with Helpline 1930 available for cyber fraud complaints.

🔹 Responsible AI Development: Under the IndiaAI Mission, the government is funding indigenous AI safety projects, including Saakshya (IIT Jodhpur & IIT Madras), AI Vishleshak, and IIT Kharagpur's Real-Time Voice Deepfake Detection System, alongside the India AI Governance Guidelines to promote safe, trusted and responsible AI deployment.

The message is clear: AI innovation is welcome, but deepfakes, impersonation, misinformation, child exploitation, and unlawful synthetic content will face significantly stricter regulation, faster takedowns, and stronger legal consequences than ever before.

That institutional role makes perceived neutrality as important as formal constitutional powers.

The video's imagined solution—dissolve the opposition, freeze their symbols and allow only one party to contest—is obviously presented as an extreme proposition.

text:
*Elon Musk’s Starlink was trying to beat Jio in India*

*But Jio used its 1st mover’s advantage to stop them in their tracks*

*The SHOCKER? Indian Gov is changing a 138 year old law that will bring Starlink back in the game*

*Here’s how Elon is rethinking internet & can possibly kill Jio:*

In 2016, when most of us were witnessing a business disruption standing in queues to get our hands on the free Jio sim card,

12,869 miles away at Rocket Road, California, a group of engineers were planning a technological disruption.

Their goal? Rethink internet access.

Their solution? Satellite Internet.

Traditionally, we have been using internet that relies on cable wires, fiber optic lines, or cellular networks.

But making cable wires or fiber optic lines available in remote villages and hard terrains is not only costly but highly impractical as well.

And this is where satellite internet and Starlink by Elon Musk comes in.

Satellite Internet uses signals from satellites orbiting the Earth.

And Starlink is a collection of thousands of small satellites orbiting around 350 miles above the Earth.

For the satellite internet to work, the user on the ground connects to the Starlink dish, known as the user terminal.

The user terminal communicates with nearby Starlink satellites and forms a link to the larger Starlink network

The satellites then form a mesh network, that allows them to pass data between each other and create global network coverage.

Starlink’s motto is — ‘virtually anywhere on earth without wires or cellphone towers.’

It started its operation in 2019 and true to its motto, it’s already available in over 65 countries,

— covering all 7 continents (including Antarctica!)

But Starlink hasn’t been able to make any progress in India.

Last year, it registered its business in India via a local unit Starlink Satellite Communications Pvt Ltd.

The company had planned to provide fast internet data in the Indian market at a subsidized price compared to the international market.

It had received 5,000+ pre-orders.

But the government said Starlink Internet Services doesn’t have the license to offer services in India.

And it asked Starlink to return people’s money.

Now, one company’s loss is another company’s gain.

In Feb this year, Reliance Jio partnered up with Luxembourg-based SES to provide satellite-based broadband services in India.

And created a joint venture called — Jio Space Technology Ltd.

Moreover, Starlink and Jio Space aren’t the only contenders for India’s space spectrum.

OneWeb is backed by Airtel in India and Hughes Communication.

Tata group entity Nelco partnered up with Canada's Telesat.

And Amazon’s Kuiper is going to launch satellites in 2024.

But why are so many companies vying for India’s space spectrum?

India has a population of 1.4 billion out of which 40% do not have internet access because they are in rural and remote areas.

And traditional terrestrial networks are not easy to install.

Hence, India’s satellite broadband service is expected to reach $1.9 billion by 2030, growing at a CAGR of 36%.

Now, because India has so many contenders for its spectrum, the question arises — who should get it?

Starlink and OneWeb wanted the government to assign licenses to companies, since spectrum is a natural resource that should be shared by companies.

But Jio wanted the government to auction the spectrum like it did with 4G & 5G 👀

Finally, the government brought in some reforms and firstly dedicated a sole agency IN-SPACe to authorize space activities for both government and private satellite communication companies.

And a bill has been proposed to replace the 138-year-old Indian Telegraph Act that currently governs the telecommunication sector.

So now, both Jio Space & OneWeb have received their GMPCS license from the Department of Telecommunications in India.

And Starlink is 3rd in line to receive the GMPCS license.

India has quietly frozen Starlink. It issued the license nearly a year ago, then let the final security clearance sit, and the whole satellite-comms sector has slowed with it. This is not a compliance dispute. New Delhi is asking a question Starlink can't really answer: given its US ownership and global network, how can it promise to follow Indian rules when Washington wants the opposite?

What spooked them is concrete. Starlink terminals were used in the Iran war even though it holds no license in Iran. India watched a sovereign state fail to switch off a network running over its own territory, and asked who is next.

Notice the tell. Jio and Bharti get an easier ride because their satellite partners are European, not a US-controlled operator. The worry isn't the satellites, it's whose hand is on the switch. And it lands days before SpaceX's IPO at a $1.75tn valuation, with Starlink as the main revenue engine, a reminder that the global rollout is far from uniform: shut out of China, and now stuck in India too.

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

text:
IFF statement on Delhi Police notices to Meta seeking the identities of creators, and the continuing removal of CJP protest content from Instagram

19 September 2026

Over the course of today, several content creators who posted about the Jantar Mantar protests have written to us after receiving an email from Meta. The email states that Meta Platforms Inc. has received "a valid legal process seeking information about your Facebook account", that it "intends to comply with the request… to the extent consistent with applicable law", and that the information sought "may include basic identifying information associated with the account". The requesting party is the Delhi Police. The email does not say under which provision the request has been made, in which FIR, for what offence, or by which officer. This is not the first request of its kind. On 27 July the Delhi Police directed platforms to remove content uploaded during the protests, and on 29 July it wrote to X seeking the names, addresses, phone numbers, email IDs and login and logout records of accounts which it said had posted "derogatory, malicious and defamatory" material about the Prime Minister.

These requests come at the end of a long process of removal which has been concentrated on Instagram, the platform on which the protest was organised and reported. Sakhi, the Jamia student whose "vastegune huia" reels went to millions, found in early August that four reels uploaded between 20 and 25 July had been restricted in India with the standard notice citing a notice from "The Government of India/Law Enforcement under section 79(3)(b)". These included a video of Delhi Police personnel unloading food from a truck after the lathi charge and an interview with Mohammed Junaid, a volunteer who distributed food at Jantar Mantar. A fifth reel, in which Sakhi described how their clothes were torn during the police action on 20 July, was removed on a different ground altogether, Instagram's community standard on "adult sexual exploitation". Gopika, the vice president of JNUSU, uploaded a screenshot of a rape threat she had received along with a note about it, and the post was removed for "sexual and nudity content". The SFI's video of Junaid was taken down under "legal requirements". Gajendra Singh's footage of a protester injured on 20 July was restricted the next day.

The same pattern is visible at news organisations. Maktoob Media's two videos on the crackdown were blocked within minutes of upload by what Instagram described as an automated system acting under the IT Rules, with no route to appeal. Scroll, The Hindu, Alt News and Peek TV have each reported posts on pellet injuries, on the doxxing of women protesters and on police conduct being restricted in India. Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka of the CJP and Arvind Kejriwal have reported the same. In every case the user who clicks "See why" is told that the action was taken "based on a local legal requirement" and nothing more. Some restrictions apply to whole accounts and not to individual posts. 

In a matter in which IFF assisted before the Delhi High Court, a creator's verified account with about 1,03,000 followers was withheld across India on the basis of a single-page, system-generated notice from a State police CID which named no post and no complainant. On 18 September Instagram restricted a post by the Software Freedom Law Centre which discussed the removal of Alt News' fact-checks. A reel on the proposed data centre in Visakhapatnam, which IFF also challenged, was restored this week after three and a half months, after the blocking order obtained in litigation turned out to allege "misinformation" about a person who does not appear in the reel. It is also worth recording that this has taken place in the weeks after Meta, having removed a post by the Prime Minister and been given three days by a parliamentary committee to apologise, sent its chief global affairs officer to Delhi to do so.

The case of the journalist Ila Kazmi shows how the system works when it is directed at reporting on the police themselves. On 23 July she published a two-part report on her Instagram account @ ilareports showing police personnel seated in a van at Jantar Mantar and matching live CCTV footage against photographs of individuals. This was the first public documentation of facial recognition being used at the protest, and IFF relied on it when it wrote to the Commissioner of Police and filed RTIs. Part 2 of the report was restricted in India on 24 July under a Section 79(3)(b) notice. On 4 September she posted a reel referring to The Indian Express's investigation into the list of 2,873 persons which the Delhi Police told the Supreme Court its facial recognition system had flagged at the protest. By the police's own preliminary assessment, 162 people on that list were lodged in prison at the time. On 9 September her entire account was withheld in India, again citing Section 79(3)(b), even as the Account Status page on the same app informed her that her account "meets all of our guidelines". She wrote to MeitY. On 15 September the Section 69A Cell of the Ministry replied that the account "is blocked under section 79(3)(b) of the IT act" and that she was "requested to take up the matter with the concerned State department". The reply does not say which State or which department. The Union ministry which administers the blocking framework has confirmed to a journalist that her account has been blocked and has declined to tell her by whom. IFF is assisting her.

Most of the people who have written to us are not employed by news organisations. They are students, freelancers and people who run one account with a few thousand followers, in some cases a lakh. They have no lawyers and no way of reaching Meta other than an in-app form which produces the same message each time. When such an account is withheld its audience disappears at once. When its owner receives an email of the kind described above, they do not know what it is or what will follow from it. It is these accounts, more than the larger outlets, which have borne the removals since July and which are now being asked to give up their identities.

IFF condemns the demand for the identities of persons who documented, satirised or commented on a public protest, and the removal of the record they created. We call on the Delhi Police to withdraw the notices and on Meta to decline to act on them and to restore the content.

On the law, there is no investigation for these notices to serve. 

On 1 September 2026, on the application of the Delhi Police itself, the Supreme Court invoked Article 142 to quash all thirteen FIRs registered in Delhi over the protests of 20 to 25 July "along with any proceedings arising therefrom". It directed that any other FIR concerning the same incidents "shall not be pursued or investigated" and shall be "taken to have been closed for all intents and purposes", and it barred the registration of any fresh FIR save one against 2,873 named individuals, confined to allegations of bodily harm and destruction of public property. 

The order records the acknowledgement of the Union and the States that "mere participation in the protests is not taken as an offence under the penal laws", and it makes the relief conditional on both sides honouring the commitments made before the Court. A notice served on an intermediary under Section 94 of the BNSS or Rule 3(1)(j) of the IT Rules is a step in an investigation, and it must be tied to one which the law permits. The Delhi Police is not the investigating agency in any of the thirteen quashed FIRs, which suggests that these requests arise from a separate FIR concerning posts about the Prime Minister. That FIR concerns the same incidents and stands closed by the order. 

In any event defamation under Section 356 of the BNS is a non-cognisable offence, and a court may take cognisance of it only on the complaint of the person aggrieved under Section 222 of the BNSS. The police have no power to investigate it of their own motion, let alone to collect the identities of those who may have committed it.

Our demands

1. The Delhi Police must withdraw every notice issued to an intermediary seeking the identity or subscriber details of any person in connection with content about the protests of 20 to 25 July 2026, and must disclose the FIR, the provision and the officer under whose authority each such notice was issued.

2. The Ministry of Home Affairs and MeitY must publish every notice issued under Section 79(3)(b) concerning content about the protests since 20 July, withdraw those directed at satire, commentary and documentation, and inform every affected person of the agency which issued the notice against them, beginning with the account @ ilareports

3. Meta must decline to act on legal process which, on the face of the Supreme Court's orders of 28 July and 1 September, has no lawful investigation behind it. It must supply to each user it has notified a copy of the process served on it. It must restore the posts, reels and accounts restricted in India since 20 July, inform each affected user of the agency and the ground on which the restriction was imposed, stop applying community standards to documentation of protests and police action, and publish figures for the notices and data requests it has received from Indian authorities since July.

4. The surveillance of protestors, through facial recognition at the site and through requests for data from intermediaries afterwards, must be placed before the Supreme Court and the HPEC. IFF will assist affected persons in doing so.

Any person who has received such an email from Meta, or whose posts, reels or account have been removed or withheld in India, can write to us at legal@internetfreedom.in. We are providing assistance on a pro bono basis.

text:
So in Delhi, apparently someone can dress up as a policeman and move around without anyone questioning it. Don’t we have to ask how that is possible?

If people allegedly dressed as police officers were able to commit such a serious offence, the question cannot stop at “they were not real policemen.” That answer, if established, raises an even more important question: why was impersonation of police officers possible in the first place, and where were the systems meant to detect it?

A few years ago, after we reported alleged demands for bribes and posted videos, one of my tweets went viral. We were subsequently approached and asked to remove it, with the explanation that the people involved were supposedly “behroopiya log”—impersonators, not police personnel.

I remember thinking then: is this a joke?

And that is why the present incident raises serious questions for me. If individuals dressed as police officers were able to move around and, as reported, assault a woman, the fact that they were allegedly impersonators does not end the accountability question. It begins another one.

Responsibility, however, must be properly assigned.

The park or land-owning authority is generally responsible for the park's maintenance, lighting, access points and any CCTV or security infrastructure under its control, including supervision of contracted services.

The police are responsible for policing, beat patrols, responding to complaints, crime prevention and investigation, and enforcement of criminal law within their jurisdiction.

Civic agencies have responsibility for the civic functions assigned to them, while contractors and security agencies are responsible for the services they have been engaged to provide, subject to oversight by the contracting authority.

Then comes accountability.

If CCTV under an agency's control was not working, who was responsible for maintaining it? Was the failure known? Was it reported? Who was monitoring it?

If a location was known or reported to be unsafe, what preventive measures were available and were they actually being implemented?

If police impersonation was involved, what systems exist to detect and respond to it?

If complaints had previously been made, were they recorded and acted upon?

And if responsibility falls between agencies, who is the nodal authority ensuring that the gap does not become an excuse for inaction?

I have personally encountered situations in South Delhi where I felt complaints received inadequate or delayed attention. I have also raised concerns about alleged demands for bribes. I am describing my experiences and concerns—not claiming that they establish misconduct by an entire institution.

There are many police officers doing difficult work every day. This is not an argument against the police. It is an argument for clear responsibility and measurable accountability.

Citizens, particularly women, should take reasonable precautions. But telling citizens to be careful cannot substitute for functioning public-safety systems.

The questions after an incident should be simple:

Who had the duty? Who was supervising it? Was the risk known? Was it reported? What action was taken? And if the responsibility was not discharged, who was held accountable?

If someone can simply put on a police uniform and walk around Delhi without attracting scrutiny, perhaps the question we should be asking is not merely “Were they really policemen?”

It is: “Why was it possible for them to appear to be?”

text:
Two Muslim women journalists on Thursday alleged that they were beaten by Delhi police personnel in South Delhi’s Saket police station. The two journalists said that a police team detained them and took them to the Saket police station, where they were assaulted.The journalists were on assignment to cover an event attended by Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta and Union Home Minister Amit Shah, following which the assault occurred, the journalists alleged. 

The journalists Shaheen Khan and Nafessa Khan alleged that they were dragged by their hair upstairs and were met with brutish assault for approximately 40 mins. 

“They dragged us upstairs by our hair and brutally assaulted us there. When they became exhausted from beating us, they stopped to take a break.”  Journalist Shaheen Khan told FoEJ Media. 

Both the journalists further claimed that on learning about their Muslim identity, the assault was intensified. 

“When they found out that we were Muslims, she said, ‘You’re Muslim? Now I’ll beat you even more'” Shaheen said. 

“She told me, ‘You’re Muslim? I’ll hit you three or four more times.’ She then struck me so hard with a lathi that the injury is still swollen.”  Nafeesa added, showing her bruises to FoEJ Media. 

Revealing the start of the assault, Shaheen said, “I was standing downstairs, speaking to my family over the phone and informing them about what had happened. Meanwhile, a female police officer approached me and demanded that I hand over my phone. When I told her, ‘Please tell me what happened; whatever you need to discuss, we can discuss it here,’ she replied, ‘I have a different way of talking. We’ll talk upstairs.’” 

“Listen to the language she used. She said, ‘I have a different way of talking. I’ll speak to you upstairs.'” Shaheen highlighted.

“She snatched my phone and started slapping me,” she added. 

Both the journalists further alleged that they were refused to have water even when they were falling to grasp the air due to the continuous assault. 

“When we asked, ‘Ma’am, please give us some water,’ she replied, ‘We will beat you thirsty,'” Shaheen alleged.

“Nafeesa’s condition deteriorated, and she collapsed unconscious. I told them that she needed medical attention, but no one paid any heed,” she added. 

The incident occurred on Thursday morning when the Union Home Minister Amit Shah and Chief Minister Rekha Gupta attended the inauguration of Max Smart Super Speciality Hospital in Saket. 

The journalist said that they had gone to cover the event; however, they were stopped by police and taken to Saket police station, where the assault was launched. 

In an official statement, DCP (South) Anant Mittal described the allegations as “factually incorrect and misleading.”

“Claims suggesting otherwise, including allegations of assault for asking questions to the Hon’ble Chief Minister, are totally false, misleading, and baseless. Citizens and social media users are advised to refrain from circulating unverified and misleading information,” read the statement.  

The police said that despite multiple requests and instructions to remove the vehicles and clear the route, they refused to remove them. Following the security and safety protocol of the VVIP route, both the journalists were taken to the local police station for the inquiry, the police said, and the Hindustan Times highlighted. 

“In recent days, 4pm has been consistently raising serious questions and publishing reports on matters related to the Delhi government and Chief Minister Rekha Gupta. In such a context, it is natural to wonder whether today’s action is connected to those reports and questions in any way.” said Sanjay Sharma, the editor-in-chief of 4pm News Network. 

“Since when has asking questions of the Chief Minister become a crime? Since when has a journalist’s question become so dangerous for those in power? And can a journalist having ‘Khan’ in their name become a reason for assaulting them?” he posted on X. 

In a statement, the Press Club of India, Indian Women’s Press Corps, Delhi Union of Journalists, Press Association, and Kerala Union of Working Journalists condemned the assault and have “called for punitive action against Delhi Police officials…for brutally assaulting [the two] freelance journalists.”

The incident was also condemned by the political leaders. Congress posted the video on X, while members of the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) have condemned the alleged use of force against journalists and accused the government of failing to protect press freedom. Indian Youth Congress leader Darshan Kaushik speaking to FoEJ Media said, “It is extremely shameful that two girls were subjected to brutality after being asked about their religion. Even today, if they have to prove their loyalty to the country and the public, it is highly shameful.”

Protests and sit-ins have also occurred outside the Saket police station, with demonstrators demanding that an FIR be registered against the police personnel allegedly involved.Two Muslim women journalists on Thursday alleged that they were beaten by Delhi police personnel in South Delhi’s Saket police station. The two journalists said that a police team detained them and took them to the Saket police station, where they were assaulted.The journalists were on assignment to cover an event attended by Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta and Union Home Minister Amit Shah, following which the assault occurred, the journalists alleged. 

The journalists Shaheen Khan and Nafessa Khan alleged that they were dragged by their hair upstairs and were met with brutish assault for approximately 40 mins. 

“They dragged us upstairs by our hair and brutally assaulted us there. When they became exhausted from beating us, they stopped to take a break.”  Journalist Shaheen Khan told FoEJ Media. 

Both the journalists further claimed that on learning about their Muslim identity, the assault was intensified. 

“When they found out that we were Muslims, she said, ‘You’re Muslim? Now I’ll beat you even more'” Shaheen said. 

“She told me, ‘You’re Muslim? I’ll hit you three or four more times.’ She then struck me so hard with a lathi that the injury is still swollen.”  Nafeesa added, showing her bruises to FoEJ Media. 

Revealing the start of the assault, Shaheen said, “I was standing downstairs, speaking to my family over the phone and informing them about what had happened. Meanwhile, a female police officer approached me and demanded that I hand over my phone. When I told her, ‘Please tell me what happened; whatever you need to discuss, we can discuss it here,’ she replied, ‘I have a different way of talking. We’ll talk upstairs.’” 

“Listen to the language she used. She said, ‘I have a different way of talking. I’ll speak to you upstairs.'” Shaheen highlighted.

“She snatched my phone and started slapping me,” she added. 

Both the journalists further alleged that they were refused to have water even when they were falling to grasp the air due to the continuous assault. 

“When we asked, ‘Ma’am, please give us some water,’ she replied, ‘We will beat you thirsty,'” Shaheen alleged.

“Nafeesa’s condition deteriorated, and she collapsed unconscious. I told them that she needed medical attention, but no one paid any heed,” she added. 

The incident occurred on Thursday morning when the Union Home Minister Amit Shah and Chief Minister Rekha Gupta attended the inauguration of Max Smart Super Speciality Hospital in Saket. 

The journalist said that they had gone to cover the event; however, they were stopped by police and taken to Saket police station, where the assault was launched. 

In an official statement, DCP (South) Anant Mittal described the allegations as “factually incorrect and misleading.”

“Claims suggesting otherwise, including allegations of assault for asking questions to the Hon’ble Chief Minister, are totally false, misleading, and baseless. Citizens and social media users are advised to refrain from circulating unverified and misleading information,” read the statement.  

The police said that despite multiple requests and instructions to remove the vehicles and clear the route, they refused to remove them. Following the security and safety protocol of the VVIP route, both the journalists were taken to the local police station for the inquiry, the police said, and the Hindustan Times highlighted. 

“In recent days, 4pm has been consistently raising serious questions and publishing reports on matters related to the Delhi government and Chief Minister Rekha Gupta. In such a context, it is natural to wonder whether today’s action is connected to those reports and questions in any way.” said Sanjay Sharma, the editor-in-chief of 4pm News Network. 

“Since when has asking questions of the Chief Minister become a crime? Since when has a journalist’s question become so dangerous for those in power? And can a journalist having ‘Khan’ in their name become a reason for assaulting them?” he posted on X. 

In a statement, the Press Club of India, Indian Women’s Press Corps, Delhi Union of Journalists, Press Association, and Kerala Union of Working Journalists condemned the assault and have “called for punitive action against Delhi Police officials…for brutally assaulting [the two] freelance journalists.”

text:
The Pothole Is Not an Accident

On the morning of Saturday, 13 June 2026, a woman named Kantha was riding her two-wheeler along the Siddapur road near Marathahalli, dropping her daughter Neha at college. It had rained heavily the night before, and the potholes had filled with water, which is the detail that makes them invisible. She hit one, lost control and fell. A school bus coming from behind ran her over. She died on the road, in front of her daughter.

A case was registered at the Whitefield traffic police station. Against the bus.

That is the whole architecture of the problem in one line. There is always a vehicle to charge. There is never a road to charge.

Kantha's death was not a freak event. In Bengaluru it is closer to a season. The National Crime Records Bureau counts deaths caused by the negligence of civic bodies, meaning bad roads, potholes, open drains, collapsing infrastructure, electrocution. Bengaluru has ranked first among Indian metros in that category for six consecutive years. Delhi, bigger and denser and not famous for good roads, recorded four in a year when Bengaluru recorded seventeen. Either Bengaluru's roads are uniquely lethal, or every other city is better at not counting.

The national picture, in passing: figures tabled in Parliament record 9,438 people killed in pothole crashes between 2020 and 2024, about five a day, the toll rising 53% across those years. The Supreme Court called such numbers frightening as far back as 2018. Yet the same table shows Andhra Pradesh, Bihar and Goa reporting zero pothole deaths in five years. Not zero potholes. Zero deaths. That is not a measurement. It is a filing decision.

A pothole death exists, legally, only if a police officer writes the word pothole into an FIR. Most do not. The crash becomes rash driving, or a hit-and-run. There is a driver to arrest and a section of the penal code that fits him. There is no section that fits an engineer who certified a road that dissolved in the first monsoon.

Bengaluru has a case that shows exactly how that works. On 6 February 2021, Tasdeeq Bushra, nineteen and in her first year of MBBS, was riding home along Hennur Main Road. She swerved to avoid a pothole. A truck hit her scooter from behind, she fell, and she went under the wheels.

The truck belonged to the Bruhat Bengaluru Mahanagara Palike. The city's own civic body owned the vehicle that killed her, and the road, and the pothole she was avoiding. The driver was arrested under Section 304A, causing death by negligence. The agency was not. Her father, Mushtaq Ahmed, put it better than any court has: "We have lost our only child. Whom will we pin the blame on? The vehicle was BBMP's and so was the driver, the roads were poorly built by them." BBMP, the water board and the electricity utility then blamed one another, which is the standard procedure.

Two details from what followed are worth sitting with. The FIR did not mention the pothole. And the pothole was filled within hours of her death. The evidence was repaired faster than the case was built.

Hers is not an outlier, it is the template. The News Minute traced thirteen pothole deaths in Bengaluru between 2017 and 2022. Families compensated: zero. Officials held accountable: zero. Not for want of a policy. BBMP had notified one, three lakh rupees for a death, and reporters found zonal chief engineers who did not know it existed and had never received a claim. A right nobody is told about is not a right, it is a press release. When Ashwin, twenty-seven, died on a pothole in MS Palya, police first blamed him for riding irresponsibly. His mother fought to get one line into the FIR naming unnamed civic officers. Nothing came of it.

The courts have been trying for a decade. A petition filed in 2015 is still running, and the High Court has reprimanded the corporation repeatedly, once issuing a contempt notice after BBMP resisted paying compensation at all. At one hearing, BBMP informed the court that Bengaluru contained 221 potholes in total. The court told it to be honest.

Then came the deadline. After a student named Dhanushree was crushed by a tipper lorry in September 2025 while swerving around a pothole, the Chief Minister announced that Bengaluru would be pothole-free by the end of October, with eleven hundred crore rupees sanctioned. Officials counted potholes by the thousand and announced them filled. The deadline was missed and replaced with another. In Whitefield, residents watched gravel tipped into holes, gravel that scatters as soon as vehicles pass over it.

Here is how that pothole-free year ended. On 20 November, three weeks after the deadline, Shantamma, forty-six, riding pillion home from work, fell on a broken stretch in Hulimavu and was run over by a truck. Police blamed potholes and loose gravel. On 17 December, Tabrez, thirty-two, swerved near Nelamangala and put his front wheel into an unbarricaded pipeline pit. He died at NIMHANS two days later. Not a pothole, strictly. The same disease.

Then the rains came back in June, and so did the holes, and so did Kantha's funeral.

The exhausting part is that the effort is real. The money is spent, the holes are counted and announced, and they return on schedule, because filling a pothole is not building a road. A pothole is the visible end of a chain: a specification diluted, a layer skipped, a bill cleared, an inspection signed. Every hole in a Bengaluru road has a name attached to it somewhere. None of those names ever reaches an FIR.

A drunk driver goes to jail. A negligent engineer gets transferred. A contractor whose road failed in ten weeks bids for the next tender. The person who dies becomes a line in a table.

Bengaluru has led that table for six years and has still not produced one official who lost a job over a death. Until a road failure is something a person can be charged with, the ritual continues: a monsoon, a hole, a two-wheeler, a bus behind it, a case against the driver, gravel by the weekend, and a family being told that what happened to them was an accident.

It was not an accident. Someone built that.

text:
The Delhi Police's takedown drive against posts critical of the Prime Minister is unconstitutional. 

New Delhi, 27 July 2026

Media reports today state that the Delhi Police has directed social media platforms to remove posts, videos, memes and reels containing remarks it describes as "abusive", "offensive" and "objectionable" towards the Prime Minister, uploaded during the student protests at Jantar Mantar and after the 'Sansad Chalo' march of 20 July 2026. At least three platforms have reportedly received notices. Several posts have already been taken down. A dedicated police team is monitoring social media to identify further content, and reports indicate that criminal proceedings are contemplated against those who posted it. No order has been published. While reports indicate the notices invoke the Information Technology Act, the specific provision relied upon and the text of the notices remain undisclosed. 

The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns this takedown drive and calls for the notices to be disclosed and withdrawn.

On the reports available, the content being removed is political expression. The movement at Jantar Mantar has been conducted as much through reels, memes, posters and digital artwork as through assembly on the ground. This is how a digital native generation raised online speaks about accountability. As per Article 19(2) restrictions on speech only on eight specified grounds. Offensiveness is not one of them. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court struck down Section 66A of the IT Act precisely because expressions such as "grossly offensive" and causing "annoyance" were vague, subjective, and swept protected speech within their net. Eleven years later, the Delhi Police is applying the same standard through informal notices and legal powers which are not being publicly disclosed. 

As per existing practices there are two routes for removing online content. The first is Section 69A of the IT Act read with the Blocking Rules, 2009, which requires a reasoned order, committee review, and notice to the originator, as the Delhi High Court affirmed in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). The second is Section 79(3)(b), which Shreya Singhal read down to require a court order or a government notification strictly confined to Article 19(2) grounds. If these notices were routed through the Sahyog Portal, they rest on a regime whose constitutionality remains under challenge before multiple High Courts. However, even if it is used police notices citing offensiveness satisfy neither. 

Reports that platforms were told the content violates "their policies" make the defect worse, the police have no mandate to enforce the community guidelines of private companies. Unpublished directions are also contrary to Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637, which requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published so that they can be challenged. If the underlying theory is defamation of the Prime Minister, the police have no role at all. Defamation under Section 356 of the BNS is a non-cognizable offence, prosecuted only on a complaint by the person aggrieved under Section 222 of the BNSS. 

Our demands

1. The Delhi Police must publish every notice issued, the legal provision invoked, and the list of URLs affected.

2. Notices directed at satire, criticism, and political commentary must be withdrawn. Any removal must follow the procedures under Section 69A or a judicial order.

3. No criminal proceedings should be initiated against persons for speech that does not meet the constitutional threshold of incitement.

4. Platforms must decline requests unsupported by valid legal orders, notify affected users, and disclose the number of government demands in their transparency reports.

Students who question an examination system are exercising their fundamental rights and deleting their posts will not delete their questions.

Reports referred to:

1. Times of India, "Delhi Police orders removal of offensive posts against PM Narendra Modi linked to NEET paper leak protests", 27 July 2026
2. News18, "Delhi Police Issues Notices To Social Media Platforms Over Offensive Posts Against PM Modi During Jantar Mantar Protest", 27 July 2026

text:
Rajput reopens the investigation into Disha, who died a week ago. 

The Bombay High Court has ordered India's Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) to re-investigate the death of Disha Salian, former manager of Bollywood actor Sushant Singh Rajput. The court reached this decision after considering a petition filed by her father, Satish Salian, who stated that the incident, which occurred six years ago, was not a suicide or an accident, but a murder committed after a gang rape.

In the first week of June 2020, during the COVID-19 pandemic, 28-year-old Disha Salian had her father call the police to inquire if she was allowed to travel for a promotional event. She showed her parents the advance payment she received and left home, saying she would return in two days. However, her father was informed by the police that she had died on the night between June 8th and 9th. Her friends stated that she had fallen from the 12th floor of a building in Mumbai and that it was an accident due to alcohol consumption, but the police later concluded it was a suicide.

However, Justices Sarang V. Kotwal and Ranjitsingh Raja Bhonsle, who heard the petition, pointed out significant inconsistencies in the police investigations conducted in two phases over more than six years. The court questioned the absence of bloodstains at the site where the body fell, the injuries mentioned in the post-mortem report not being consistent with a fall from a height, and the delay in police documentation. Furthermore, the court severely criticized the investigation of this incident merely as a suspicious death from the outset, without registering a First Information Report (FIR) in the casebook.

According to a complaint filed by Satish Salian, the Central Bureau of Investigation has now registered a new FIR. Disha, who worked at KWAN Entertainment, had come to know about illegal activities including drug trafficking and child abuse involving a former minister and several others, and she had provided this information to Sushant Singh Rajput. Her father alleges that since they were preparing to reveal this information through a press conference, this planned crime was committed and evidence destroyed to protect powerful individuals in the relevant jurisdiction.

Less than a week after Disha's death, actor Sushant Singh Rajput was also found dead at his home, and the police concluded that his death was also a suicide. Sushant's girlfriend, Rhea Chakraborty, was arrested, but later CBI investigations revealed that she or her family had no connection to it, and the case was closed last year. However, Disha's father states that both these deaths are connected.

The court's decision states that the registration of this new FIR does not determine anyone as guilty, nor does it consider anyone a suspect until sufficient evidence is received. However, due to the involvement of prominent politicians, senior police officers, and Bollywood actors, this incident has once again become a major news story in India amidst political criticism and accusations.

text:
Dear @raghav_chadha ,

I know you are doing very well in Parliament by raising small issues that were ignored by most Members of Parliament but have a bigger impact.

I am writing this post regarding an account lien and bank freeze by the Cyber Police of India.

In my case, the issue started when I received a message from my bank branch stating that my account had received a police notice of lien of 6000 rupees. I immediately went to my bank branch and asked them why my account had a lien of 6000 rupees. They followed some procedure and gave me a printout which contained the acknowledgement of my lien. One of the bank employees told me that I should contact the cyber police mentioned on the paper and provide them with the details of the 6000 rupees, such as where it came from and for what reason. However, they did not give me any specific reason why my bank account had received the lien.

Later, I checked my bank statement to find the details of the 6000 rupees transaction and noticed that my case was reported on 6 December 2025, and I had received a transaction of 6000 rupees on the same date. I remember that my neighbour had sent me this 6000 rupees and asked me to withdraw it from the ATM because he had an urgent situation as his mother was going to her village due to an emergency. As a friend, I withdrew the money and gave it to him.

Now I have all the proofs and details to explain to the police, so I emailed all the details to the Bangalore Cyber Cell or the police station where my notice was issued, as mentioned in the acknowledgement given by my bank. However, I did not receive any response. I then tried to contact the investigation officer mentioned in the report. I called several times, keeping a gap of five to six hours out of respect for his time and duties, as they may have many other responsibilities. I also sent him a message on WhatsApp, but there was still no response.

After four to five days, I called again, and this time he picked up the call. He was speaking in the local language, which I did not understand, as I am from Maharashtra and not familiar with the local language of Bangalore. I then started speaking in English, and he told me that I have to come to Bangalore and verify my documents. I explained that for 6000 rupees, it would not be beneficial for me to travel to Bangalore because transportation, food, and stay would cost more than 6000 rupees. He said that he does not know and that I have to come, otherwise he will not issue the No Objection Certificate, and then he ended the call.

This issue may look small, but similar issues are happening everywhere, and no one is noticing them. It feels like “Kare koi aur bhare koi.” Many innocent people face this issue, and it remains unresolved. Because of chain transactions that come into accounts, some people are unable to use their own money. If I travel, I will have to spend more than 6000 rupees to remove the lien. I believe this issue can be resolved through email or online verification, but the investigation officer denied it.

I am also tagging Pushpendra Sir @pushpendrakum and Bangalore Cyber Police @BlrCityPolice . If you could please look into this matter.

Thank you.

@Meta @NCPCR @MeitY @JoelKaplan Tracked by Press Monitor — today's press review covers four major developments in social media regulation and platform governance.

Meta has agreed to report child safety cases directly to the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre, bypassing the US-based NCMEC. This marks the first time a major technology intermediary has established a direct reporting channel with Indian law enforcement. The move follows government warnings that online safety of children is non-negotiable and platforms failing to take proactive measures will face appropriate action.

The European Union is proposing the EU Kids Act, which would ban minors under 15 from opening accounts on social media, video-sharing platforms, chatbots, and online games. The tiered access system under parental supervision would require digital platforms to be safe by design for children — the most sweeping child safety regulation proposed by any major economy.

The National Commission for Protection of Child Rights has summoned Meta India's managing director for a formal inquiry into child sex abuse content on the platform, escalating regulatory scrutiny after Meta's reply to its earlier notice.

The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology raised CSAM data sharing concerns with Meta's Joel Kaplan, noting that slow data sharing delayed critical investigations and left children unprotected. MeitY insists CSAM instances must go directly to Indian law enforcement.

text:
Why MAGA hates Indians more than Muslim immigrants

My cousin in Australia bought a $100,000 yellow Mustang GT. Before the car was insured, he made the mistake of parking it kerbside instead of in the garage. Four local youths stole the car, drag raced it down to its rims, and burned it. The police had to let them go. My cousin got $0 as insurance. Just to piss the youth off, he bought the exact same Mustang the next day. He saw the 4 youths walking past his house and looking enviously at his brand new car. Imagine the resentment he would have created simply by existing. Muslim immigrants rarely evoke such feelings.

Aussies are really cool and welcoming people. The four youths could have been hoons in any country and are not representative of Australians.  I mentioned this episode only to highlight the fact that success can breed envy. My own family members in Kerala who drive Mercs become envious at simple things like my professional achievements or if I post a picture of myself with Mr D.

My point is that envy is universal. So let's transpose it on MAGA. Indians in the West, especially the US where the most educated Indians live, compete for white collar jobs - lawyers, doctors, software engineers, finance, media. In stark contrast, Bangladeshis, Pakistanis, Afghans, Syrians, Libyans, Egyptians, Somalis, Sudanese, Algerians, Iraqis, Palestinians, Iranians and Tunisians take up jobs like furniture removers, airport baggage handlers, couriers, sanitation workers, etc - jobs that do not directly threaten local people's livelihoods.

So while Indian immigrants won't ever physically attack a local Westerner or join an Islamic terrorist group or blow up people, an Indian immigrant competes with locals for a shrinking pool of white collar  jobs. For the irrational human mind that feels more of an immediate threat than an annual terrorist attack on a Christmas market or the bombing of a gay nightclub. Plus, liberals love Muslims.

Most Muslims in the West live in ghettoes. Whereas an Indian doctor might move into the million dollar home next door.

For those long used to seeing Indians as the Apu 7/11 stereotype, an Indian is no longer a joke but a threat. That can be upsetting on many levels. In 2008 when India sent a spacecraft that did a hard landing on the moon, Fox News published this headline: "Whoa, where did they learn to do that." The headline was taken down a few hours later.

However, I wouldn't tar everyone with the same brush. Italian and Irish immigrants in America faced horrible levels of parochialism and violence from the original settlers. But both groups were integrated after being coopted as whites. Indians cannot become white for obvious reasons but over the long term, integration is as inevitable as day following night. And MAGA can stop it like they can stop the sun from rising.
